figures.title: Aligned rounding errors add linearly; independent errors add in quadrature
figures.caption: With N = 4,096 terms, a half-step of 0.067, and an input RMS of 0.5, aligned errors would add to 4,096 × 0.0335 = 137.2. Independent errors add in quadrature: the worst case is √4,096 × 0.0335 = 2.14, and uniform rounding gives a per-term standard deviation of (step/√12) × x_rms ≈ 0.0192, so √4,096 × 0.0192 ≈ 1.23. The ratio between the linear and quadrature totals is 64, the square root of N.
figures.alt: Three horizontal bars. The aligned-error bar is 137.2 and fills the plot. The independent worst case is 2.14, and the uniform-rounding estimate is 1.23; both are short bars, roughly one sixty-fourth of the first. The caption gives the arithmetic: 4,096 × 0.0335, √4,096 × 0.0335, and √4,096 × 0.0192.

data.note: The ratio is 64 = √4,096. Aligned errors share a sign; independent errors cancel in quadrature.

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to compare a linear error sum with a quadrature one.

steps.label: The dot product has N = 4,096 terms, each half-step is 0.067, and the input RMS is 0.5, so a term's typical error magnitude is 0.067/2 x 0.5 = 0.0335. If every error and every input shared a sign, the totals would add linearly: 4,096 x 0.0335 = 137.2.
Independent zero-mean errors add in quadrature instead: sqrt(4,096) x 0.0335 = 64 x 0.0335 = 2.14.
Uniform rounding gives a per-term standard deviation of (step/sqrt(12)) x x_rms ≈ 0.0385 x 0.5 ≈ 0.0192, so the quadrature total is sqrt(4,096) x 0.0192 ≈ 1.23.
The ratio between the linear and quadrature totals is 64, the square root of N: independence is worth a factor of 64 on the same per-term error.

figures.title: Group size and bit width set the rounding floor
figures.caption: A symmetric four-bit group with m = 4.0 has step 2·4/15 ≈ 0.533, so 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 all round to 0.2667. Put 4.0 in its own group and the remaining weights get m = 0.3 and step 0.04, so 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 land on distinct levels. The floor is set by the bit width: at four bits the step is m/7 and the half-step ≈ 0.2σ; at three bits the step is m/3 and the half-step ≈ 0.43σ; at two bits the step is m and the half-step ≈ 1σ. Smaller groups isolate outliers, at the cost of more scale metadata.
figures.alt: Three aligned panels. The first has one group containing 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, and 4.0, with m = 4.0 and step 0.533; the three small weights all round to 0.2667. The second puts 4.0 alone and gives the remaining group m = 0.3 and step 0.04, so 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 land on distinct levels. The third gives the step and half-step at four, three, and two bits: step m/7 with half-step ≈ 0.2σ, step m/3 with half-step ≈ 0.43σ, and step m with half-step ≈ 1σ, so four bits is close to the floor.

panels.title: bit width sets the floor
items: at half-step ≈ σ, rounding is a different function
panels.note: Four bits is an empirical default, not a theorem; quality depends on group size and model.

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to watch an outlier set a group's grid, then to read the bit-width floor.

steps.label: A group holds 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 4.0. The outlier sets m = 4.0, so the step is 2 x 4/15 ≈ 0.533 and the grid is built for a value no ordinary weight reaches.
Every ordinary weight rounds to the same level: 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 all land on 0.2667. The group keeps four bits of storage and almost none of resolution.
Split the outlier into its own group and the remaining three get m = 0.3, a step of 0.04, and distinct levels. Separate scales per block confine the damage to the block that holds the outlier.
Bit width sets the floor. At four bits the step is m/7, so with the largest weight near 3σ the half-step is about 0.2σ.
At three bits the step is m/3 and the half-step is about 0.43σ.

At two bits the step is m and the half-step is about 1σ. Once the half-step reaches σ, rounding stops being a perturbation and becomes a different function, which is why four is an empirical default rather than a theorem.
